intro: Gmail for public relations specialists on Mac runs in Safari or Chrome. Google has no official Gmail desktop app for Mac, so the browser is the main route. Install Gmail as a web app, then turn on templates and keyboard shortcuts. This page covers the setup, the pitch rules reporters care about, and where Lazur helps while you work.

blocks.text: How Gmail runs on a Mac for PR work

Gmail on a Mac means a browser or a mail app. Mailbird and Clean Email both report that Google has no official Mac desktop app. Both sell Mac email clients, so read their claim with that in mind. Google's help pages do not address that claim, so check it again before you plan around it.

For PR work, the browser route covers most needs. You get templates, filters, keyboard shortcuts, and full search across your threads. The main choice is whether you want Gmail's own layout or a mail app with a different one.
Ways to open Gmail on a Mac

items: Gmail in Safari or Chrome at mail.google.com. Open it in a normal tab, next to your research and clip links.
A Gmail web app, installed from Safari or Chrome. It gets its own window and Dock icon.
Apple Mail, added through Mail > Add Account. Gmail labels appear as mailboxes.
A third-party client such as Mimestream. It supports only Gmail.

blocks.text: Most PR specialists pick the browser or the web app. Both keep Gmail's templates and shortcuts. Apple Mail and Mimestream change how your inbox looks and sorts. Test either one on real mail before you switch.
Install Gmail as a web app in Safari or Chrome
A web app gives your press inbox its own window. You can switch to it with ⌘ Tab. It stays apart from the tabs you use for research, clip checks, and a reporter's website.

items: In Chrome, open the menu, then go to More Tools > Create Shortcut.
Check Open as window, then confirm the shortcut.
In Safari, open mail.google.com, then choose File > Add to Dock.
Open the new icon and sign in with the account you use for press work.

blocks.title: Keep press and personal mail apart
blocks.text: Use the web app only for work. Keep your personal Gmail in a normal browser tab. Separate windows make it harder to pitch from the wrong account, which can cost you a reporter's trust.
Turn on keyboard shortcuts and templates

Features that help with pitching stay off until you switch them on. Keyboard shortcuts and templates both live in Settings. Shortcuts do nothing until you enable them. Templates do not appear in Compose until you turn them on in Advanced.

To enable templates, click the gear icon, choose See all settings, then open Advanced. Turn on Templates and save your changes before you leave the page. For shortcuts, open See all settings, go to General, and turn on keyboard shortcuts.

blocks.text: On a Mac, ⌘ replaces Ctrl in every Gmail shortcut. So ⌘ Enter sends the message. Shortcuts pay off when you handle many threads in a row. Press c to start a new pitch, write it, then press ⌘ Enter.
Build pitch templates you can reuse in Gmail

A template saves a draft you have already written. You insert it later into a new message. For PR work, the best templates are short and tied to one beat or one story type. A template for every reporter on your list is the wrong goal.

items: Write the full pitch in Compose, including the subject line.
Click More options, then choose Templates > Save draft as template.
Select Save as new template, and name it by beat or story type.
Open a new message, insert the template, and read it once before you trust it.

blocks.text: To update a template, write the new version in Compose. Save it as a template again, then select the existing template. Check the name first, so you overwrite the right one.

blocks.title: Deleting is permanent
blocks.text: Templates > Delete template removes the template for good. Google says you cannot recover it after deletion. Copy the text into a note or a document before you delete anything.
Google's help pages do not say whether templates can be shared. A third-party guide says they cannot. Treat that as unverified. Ask your team before you build a shared process around templates.
Write pitches that reporters do not delete

Reporters delete pitches for reasons you can fix. In a 2025 Muck Rack survey of over 1,500 journalists, as reported by PRNEWS, 86% cited irrelevance. The same survey found 71% cited an overly promotional tone.

50% said the pitch felt like a mass email. 43% said it was too long. 33% pointed to missing or unverifiable sources. These are self-reported survey results, and the Muck Rack studies are vendor-run with self-selected samples. Treat them as a signal, not a law.

The 2026 State of Journalism survey, as reported by PR Daily, found 47% say PR pitches are seldom or never relevant to their work. PR Daily does not state the sample size on that page, so read the number with care.

Response rates are harder to hear. Propel's 2021 research, based on over one million pitches, found journalists respond to roughly 3.27% of pitches. That is about 1 in 31. Most of your pitches will get no reply, so write each one for one specific reporter.

Personal one-to-one emails still lead for most PR work. Meltwater cites Muck Rack's 2023 research, which says about 90% of PR professionals prefer one-to-one emails. Those emails support personal introductions, tracking, and file sharing.
A pitch checklist for Gmail

items: Open with the reporter's beat and one recent story they wrote.
Lead with the news. Put your second point in a single line.
Link to the data or the document, not a summary of it.
Keep the body short enough to read on a phone.
Check every name, outlet, and title before you press ⌘ Enter.
End with one clear ask, such as an interview slot or a yes or no.
Send from the address the reporter already knows.

blocks.text: Use this list as a final pass, not a rewrite. If a pitch fails any item, fix that item before you send. Then read the first line one more time.
Follow up once, in the same thread
50% of journalists say one follow-up is fine. PRNEWS adds that it is ideally sent three to seven days after the first email. That window is narrow, so set a reminder when you send the pitch.

Reply in the same thread so the reporter sees your original pitch below the new note. Keep the follow-up to a few lines. Say what is new, such as a fresh data point, a date, or a spokesperson's availability. Do not paste the whole pitch again.
Here is how a week can look. You send a pitch on Monday. You set a reminder for Thursday. On Thursday you open the original thread, add a short note with the new detail, and send it.
If the reporter does not reply after one follow-up, stop. Log the outcome in a note so the next person on the account knows what happened. A quiet no is still useful information.
Filters and auto replies: where PR teams go wrong

Gmail can send a template automatically. Create a filter that matches the messages you want, check Send template, choose the template, then click Create filter. Google's help says automatic replies with templates need a search filter.

For press, be careful with automatic replies. A template that answers every email matching a search can look like spam to a reporter. Use filters only for predictable messages, such as a known press request, and review them regularly.

blocks.title: Check matches first
blocks.text: A filter can reply to more people than you expect. Look at which messages match before you turn it on. Turn off any filter that sends replies to press you did not plan to answer.
Apple Mail and Mimestream for Gmail on Mac

Apple Mail works with Gmail, but it behaves differently. It maps Gmail labels to mailboxes, not labels. It does not show the Primary, Social, and Promotions tabs. If you sort press from newsletters with those tabs, the browser is the safer choice.

Mimestream supports only Gmail. Its main advantage is that it reads and writes filters stored in your Google account. Clean Email reports it has no free version after the trial. Check Mimestream's own pricing page before you buy.
Where Lazur helps while you work in Gmail

Lazur is a voice assistant that lives in the notch on your Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and it answers out loud. Lazur points, explains, and guides you one click at a time. It does not click buttons or operate Gmail for you.

Lazur fits best when Gmail is the thing you need help with. The menus are unfamiliar, the thread is long, or the reply needs a quick check. You decide what gets sent. You read the draft, then you press ⌘ Enter.
Ask Lazur where things are and how to do them

Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen. Ask how to do something, and it guides you one click at a time. It waits for each click before it moves on. That suits Gmail, where menus can change without notice.

blocks.text: Research is a background job. Lazur runs it in its own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension. It returns a summary and a report when it finishes. Lazur does not use the tabs you have open for this.
Dictate replies with fn, then check names
Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. In Gmail, that puts a reply straight into the message box. Dictation is unlimited on both the Pro and Power plans.

Dictation helps most with longer replies, such as a status update for a client. Snippets, a personal dictionary, and clipboard slots save more time when you repeat the same lines. Add reporter names, outlet names, and client product names to the personal dictionary.

blocks.title: Read before you send
blocks.text: Dictation can mishear a name or a figure. A wrong outlet name is hard to fix once a reporter has read it. Read every dictated line, then press ⌘ Enter.
Mistakes that cost PR specialists replies

items: Pitching a whole list at once without checking relevance.
Sending a template with the wrong reporter's name still in the greeting.
Following up again and again. Only 50% say one follow-up is fine, so more is a risk.
Putting embargoed details in a thread with other reporters on it.
Deleting a template before copying its text somewhere safe.
Turning on an auto reply filter that answers press without review.
Leaving keyboard shortcuts off, then wondering why c does nothing.

blocks.text: Most of these come from speed. Slow down on the first line of each pitch. The rest tends to get better once that line is right.
Privacy: what Lazur sees on your screen

Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. When you ask a question, the audio and a screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.
This matters for PR work. Embargoed drafts and unpublished client news may be on screen. Release the shortcut when you finish, and close or hide sensitive threads before you ask a question.
Try Lazur with your Gmail for three days
Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card. The trial starts the first time you open the app. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.

items: Pro: $18/month, or $15/month billed annually. Includes 150 AI actions.
Power: $120/month, or $96/month billed annually. Includes 1,000 AI actions.
Dictation is unlimited on both plans.

blocks.text: Test the trial on a real thread, such as one pitch and one follow-up. Price matters less than whether the answers help with your actual Gmail work. Check the full details on the [pricing page](/pricing), or start with the [download page](/download).
Next steps for your Gmail setup this week

items: Install Gmail as a web app in Safari or Chrome.
Turn on keyboard shortcuts and templates in Settings.
Save your best pitch as a template, then test it on yourself.
Set a reminder for the follow-up window, three to seven days after each pitch.
Ask Lazur to walk you through one task from the table above.

blocks.text: If you need to fix a send you regret, read [how to undo send in Gmail on Mac](/how-to/undo-send-in-gmail). Founders who write to investors can read [Gmail for founders on Mac](/for/founders/gmail).

faq.question: Is there a Gmail app for Mac?
faq.answer: Mailbird and Clean Email both report that Google has no official Gmail desktop app for Mac. Use Gmail in Safari or Chrome, or install it as a web app. Apple Mail can also connect to Gmail through Mail > Add Account.

faq.question: Can I use Gmail templates on a Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Google's help page says you can only turn on and use message templates from Gmail on your computer, and a Mac browser counts. Enable them under Settings > See all settings > Advanced.

faq.question: Can I share a Gmail template with my team?
faq.answer: Google's help pages do not say. A third-party guide says templates cannot be shared. Treat that as unverified and check before you rely on sharing.

faq.question: How long should I wait before following up with a journalist?
faq.answer: PRNEWS reports that 50% of journalists say one follow-up is fine, ideally three to seven days after the first email. Send one follow-up in the same thread, then stop unless the reporter replies.

faq.question: What makes journalists delete a pitch?
faq.answer: In Muck Rack's 2025 survey of over 1,500 journalists, as reported by PRNEWS, 86% cited irrelevance. 71% cited an overly promotional tone, and 50% said the pitch felt like a mass email.

faq.question: Does Lazur send emails for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur drafts and types text, and it guides you one click at a time. It does not click buttons or operate Gmail for you. You read the draft and press ⌘ Enter yourself.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my whole screen all the time?
faq.answer: No. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored.

faq.question: Is Mimestream a good Gmail app for PR work?
faq.answer: It supports only Gmail, and its main advantage is that it reads and writes filters stored in your Google account. Clean Email reports it has no free version after the trial. Check Mimestream's own pricing page before you buy.
